name: Teduglutide
used_for: FDA-labeled (Gattex) for adults and children aged 1 year and older with short bowel syndrome who depend on parenteral support (intravenous nutrition or fluids). It is a glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) analog. The label calls for colonoscopy and lab checks before and during treatment. Not promoted or approved for general gut health.

entries.text: Label: 0.05 mg/kg once daily by subcutaneous injection, rotating sites among the abdomen, thighs and upper arms.
entries.population: Adults and children 1 year and older with short bowel syndrome who need parenteral support

entries.text: Label: 0.025 mg/kg once daily for moderate or severe renal impairment and end-stage renal disease (eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2).
entries.population: Adults and children with moderate to severe renal impairment

internet_claims.claim: Patient reviews on WebMD describe Gattex as effective for some, with stoma growth and quick onset reported, but also stomach pain, bloating, nausea, dehydration and stoma problems; one reviewer had suspected bowel obstructions, and some stopped it.

research.summary: DailyMed prescribing information for Gattex (teduglutide) for injection, Takeda (revised September 2025).
research.finding: Approved for short bowel syndrome dependent on parenteral support in adults and children 1 year and older; gives 0.05 mg/kg daily dosing, a lower dose in renal impairment, and calls for colonoscopy and lab monitoring.

research.summary: 24-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of teduglutide 0.10 or 0.05 mg/kg daily versus placebo in 83 adults with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure (Jeppesen et al., Gut; NCT00172185).
research.finding: The 0.05 mg/kg dose significantly raised the response rate (16 of 35) versus placebo (1 of 16, p=0.007), while the 0.10 mg/kg dose did not reach significance. Three treated patients were weaned off parenteral support. Intestinal villus height and lean body mass increased.

research.summary: 24-week phase III trial in 59 children with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure: two blinded teduglutide doses versus a non-blinded standard-of-care group (Kocoshis et al., JPEN).
research.finding: At least 20% reduction in parenteral support occurred in 54.2% (0.025 mg/kg) and 69.2% (0.05 mg/kg) versus 11.1% with standard care. A few children (2 and 3) reached full enteral autonomy. Pyrexia and vomiting were the most common adverse events. The standard-of-care arm was small (9) and not blinded.
